source: Laurence & Macedo (2023) Cognitive strategies in matrix-reasoning tasks: State of the art
finding: Review of the whole field. Snow (1978, 1980) and Bethell-Fox et al. (1984) define constructive matching (build an ideal answer, then find it) and response elimination (compare features of each option to the stem and delete). Vigneau et al. (2006) turned this into eye-tracking indices. The review says the founding two-strategy paradigm still needs confirmation.
numbers: Eye-tracking samples 34 to 137 people; all studies 34 to 1,890. Example trial: 4 matrix-answer toggles (constructive) vs 11 (elimination).
quote: seems to involve the construction of an idealized answer which is compared to the response alternatives
limits: Mostly university samples. Few research groups. Methods (eye, mouse, self-report, think-aloud) never cross-validated against each other.
agent_relevance: S3/S4: the build-then-check vs eliminate contrast is a real, measurable behavioural split, but the literature admits the pure elimination type is poorly established.

source: Bethell-Fox, Lohman & Snow (1984) Adaptive reasoning: componential and eye movement analysis of geometric analogy performance
finding: Founding study. On A:B::C:D geometric analogies, higher-ability people used constructive matching and lower-ability people used response elimination. Strategy shifted with difficulty: harder items pushed people toward elimination. Known only through Laurence & Macedo 2023 and Gonthier & Roulin 2020; original not opened.
numbers: Exact N and effect sizes not recorded (original not read).
limits: Secondary report only. 4-option analogies, not 8-option 3x3 matrices.
agent_relevance: The ability-by-difficulty interaction is the prediction later work tests; elimination is a fallback when building fails.

source: Vigneau, Caissie & Bors (2006) Eye-movement analysis demonstrates strategic influences on intelligence
finding: Defined the standard indices on Raven APM: proportional time on matrix, latency to first fixation on answers, matrix-answer toggles, matrix time distribution index. More matrix time, longer latency and fewer toggles went with higher scores. Known via Laurence & Macedo 2023.
numbers: Four regression models explained 32%, 30%, 49% and 51% of APM score variance. N about 55 (per Gonthier & Roulin 2020).
limits: Small sample; variance claims are in-sample; opened only via review.
agent_relevance: Gives behavioural proxies for a log of our agent: how long it works the stem before looking at options, and how often it flips back and forth.

source: Gonthier & Roulin (2020) Intra-individual strategy shifts in Raven's matrices, and their dependence on working memory capacity and need for cognition
finding: Two samples of 100. After every APM item people self-rated both strategies. Constructive matching fell and response elimination rose steadily as items got harder. The item-level strategy index (CM minus RE) tracked accuracy almost one to one.
numbers: N=200 (2x100). Item-level r(34): CM with accuracy .82, RE with accuracy -.85, CM with RE -.77, strategy index with accuracy .89 (78% of item variance). Split-half timecourse r: .83 (CM), .85 (RE). Only people high in both working memory and need for cognition kept constructive matching late in the test.
quote: participants tended to turn to the less costly response elimination strategy as the difficulty of the task increased
limits: Self-report after each item, one question per strategy. Correlational. Young French students. Authors say people may mix both strategies within one item.
agent_relevance: Strong, large-sample support that elimination is what happens when construction fails. For S3/S4: switch to elimination only when a built answer is not reached, and treat it as lower-accuracy.

source: Gonthier & Thomassin (2015) Strategy use fully mediates the relationship between working memory capacity and performance on Raven's matrices
finding: Causal test. Experiment 1 (N=250) made half the people build the answer first: matrix alone for at least 15 s, then the 8 options appeared. This raised scores and weakened the working-memory link. Experiment 2 (N=93) showed strategy self-report fully mediated the WMC-APM link.
numbers: Exp 1: constructive n=116, control n=134. 18 odd APM items. Mean 12.77 (SD 2.35) vs 10.45 (SD 3.70), F(1,246)=37.40, partial eta2=.13. WMC-score r fell from .34 to .20; shared variance 11.6% to 4%. Interaction F(1,246)=4.80, p=.029, partial eta2=.02. Exp 2: full mediation.
quote: Inducing all participants to use an effective strategy in Raven's matrices decreased the correlation between working memory capacity and performance
limits: Interaction is small (eta2=.02, p=.029). Mediation was not replicated with a time limit (see b06). Odd items only; students only.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for the intervention: make the agent commit to a built answer BEFORE it sees the options. That lifted scores by about 2.3 of 18 items (about 0.7 SD of the control group) and cut dependence on raw capacity.

source: Jastrzebski, Ciechanowska & Chuderski (2018) Strategy use and working memory on Raven-type matrices (time-limited, larger sample)
finding: A larger time-limited sample failed to find that strategy use mediates the WMC-Gf link. This is the main non-replication of full mediation. Known via Laurence & Macedo 2023 and Gonthier & Roulin 2020; original not opened.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Time-limited APM. Gonthier & Roulin argue time pressure suppresses strategy variability, so the failure is only partly informative. Jarosz et al. argue questionnaires are a weak measure. Title is approximate.
agent_relevance: Strategy effects depend on testing conditions. Under tight budgets the build/eliminate split may matter less.

source: Jarosz, Raden & Wiley (2019) Working memory capacity and strategy use on the RAPM
finding: Think-aloud coding instead of questionnaires. Found a hybrid 'isolate-and-eliminate' strategy: find one rule, remove options by it, then seek the next rule. Pure elimination was rare. Partial (not full) mediation of WMC-Gf by strategy. Known via Laurence & Macedo 2023.
numbers: Over 50% constructive matching; about 3% pure response elimination; the rest hybrid or guessing (per review).
limits: Think-aloud lowers accuracy and coding is subjective. Original not opened. Author list approximate.
agent_relevance: S3/S4 should not be a hard fork. A rule-by-rule build that prunes options with each partial rule is the common human middle path.

source: Mitchum & Kelley (2010) Solve the problem first: constructive solution strategies can influence the accuracy of retrospective confidence judgments
finding: Forcing people to solve before seeing options raised accuracy and confidence on Raven items. Known via Laurence & Macedo 2023. Original not opened.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Secondary report only. Title approximate.
agent_relevance: Pair a build-first step with a confidence check: building makes the confidence signal more trustworthy.

source: Loesche, Wiley & Hasselhorn (2015) How knowing the rules affects solving the Raven Advanced Progressive Matrices Test
finding: Telling people the rules beforehand made them spend more time on the matrix and less on checking answers, so more constructive. Known via Laurence & Macedo 2023.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Secondary report only.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that supplies a rule vocabulary (progression, XOR, constant) before options is aligned with this.

source: Hayes, Petrov & Sederberg (2015) Do we really become smarter when our fluid-intelligence test scores improve?
finding: 35 students took APM short forms twice. Scanpath changes (more systematic row scanning, less answer checking) explained about a third of the test-retest gain. With strategy partialled out, the gain was no longer significant.
numbers: N=35. Cross-validated R2=.32 (fit R2=.56) for relational score gain from scanpath change. Practice effect after partialling: t(34)=.30 (whole group), t(10)=.25 (high improvers). Earlier work: about 40% of APM variance predicted from eye fixations (Hayes et al. 2011).
limits: Small N. Scanpath model overfits easily. Does not prove strategy is the only route to the gain.
agent_relevance: Score gains on matrix tests can be strategy refinement, not more reasoning power. Prompt gains on matrices may be exactly this.

source: Gonthier (2023) Should intelligence tests be speeded or unspeeded? A brief review of the effects of time pressure on response processes and an empirical study with Raven's matrices
finding: Random assignment to untimed, 20 min or 10 min for 18 APM items. Even mild time pressure lowered accuracy, confidence and constructive matching, beyond just going faster. Reliability fell below .70 in the 10-min group.
numbers: N=295 (97/99/99). Accuracy effect d=0.35 even with item response time controlled. Only untimed vs 20 min was significant for accuracy and confidence. Constructive matching lower under pressure; response elimination also lower (more skipping or guessing). Calibration no different: M=.47/.44/.43.
limits: Strategy measured by two self-report items per trial. Students only. The author calls the strategy effect limited in size.
agent_relevance: Time or token budgets cut construction first. If our agent has a thinking budget, expect a fall-back to option-checking or guessing; protect the build step when the budget is tight.

source: Liu, He, Man & Zhan (2025) Exploring critical eye-tracking metrics for identifying cognitive strategies in Raven's APM
finding: Re-analysis of Liu et al. (2023) data, N=192 students, 36 items. Random forest picked proportional time on matrix, latency to first toggle and its rate as the best strategy indicators. Constructive matching was used more by better scorers and less on harder items.
numbers: N=192 (147 F, 45 M), age 22.06. Spearman between item difficulty and number using elimination: .58 (p<.01). Person level r=.33 (p<.01) between count of constructive-matching items and score. K-means clusters agreed 82% with model-based labels.
limits: Labels are model-inferred, not ground truth. The paper says there is no consensus on the best metrics. A third isolate-and-eliminate class appears. Person-level r=.33 is modest.
agent_relevance: Supports the hybrid view. Person-level strategy is a modest predictor of score (r about .3), much weaker than the item-level fit in b04.

source: Liu et al. (2023) Using a multi-strategy eye-tracking psychometric model to measure intelligence and identify cognitive strategy in Raven's matrices
finding: Model with a strategy-selection part and a strategy-implementation part. Built-in assumption: constructive matching never yields lower success than elimination, with a per-item gain term. Known via Liu et al. 2025.
numbers: Exact fit not read here.
limits: The assumption is built in, not tested. Opened only via a later paper.
agent_relevance: A formal template for our own scoring: P(correct) is a mixture over strategies, with strategy chosen by cues.

source: von Gugelberg & Troche (2025) Individual differences in strategy and the item-position effect in reasoning ability measures
finding: N=210 on APM with eye tracking and bifactor fixed-links models. Constructive matching tied to reasoning ability. Change in strategy across the test tied to item position, not to ability. Metrics gave different directions: toggle rate suggested more constructive matching late; first-fixation timing suggested less.
numbers: N=210. Correlations reported for different item cut-offs (for example r=-.256 in one model, r=.529 in another). Three metrics disagreed on the direction of change.
limits: Metric disagreement is a real threat: the strategy construct may not be one thing. Results depend on cut-off.
agent_relevance: Do not assume one strategy dial. Our agent logs (time on stem, toggles, first look at options) may disagree; use more than one.

source: von Gugelberg (2026) Individual differences in problem-solving behavior in reasoning tests: the role of item difficulty and item position
finding: 300 people, figural matrices, Bayesian multilevel models. Higher reasoning ability went with lower toggle rate, more time on the matrix and later first look at answers. High-reasoning people adapted behaviour more to changing demands. Visuospatial working memory effects were selective. Between-person variance by item position exceeded that by item difficulty.
numbers: N=300. Three indices: toggle rate, proportional time on matrix, proportional time to first fixation on answers.
limits: Mainly abstract and framing read. Observational.
agent_relevance: High scorers flex strategy to the item. A fixed pipeline loses to a controller that adapts the amount of building to item difficulty.

source: Niebaum & Munakata (2023) The development of relational reasoning: an eyetracking analysis of strategy use and adaptation in children and adults
finding: 6- and 9-year-olds and adults on 24 APM items. Scanning across rows and columns predicted good performance; fast, frequent checking of answers predicted poor performance. Adapting to difficulty (more scanning, more answer consulting on hard items) predicted better scores.
numbers: Number of relations vs accuracy r=.58 (9-year-olds), r=.39 (6-year-olds, marginal). Matrix difficulty vs response time r=.86 (adults), .82 (9y), .48 (6y). Toggle count vs response time r=.85. Six-year-olds below chance often picked a duplicate answer; more elimination predicted duplicates.
limits: Mostly white, middle to high SES US sample. Strategy inferred from gaze. Adults and 9-year-olds also raised answer consulting on harder items, so more checking is not always bad.
agent_relevance: Row and column scanning (systematic relation extraction) is the good signal. Make the agent state row and column relations explicitly.

source: Hannon (2026) Sources of individual differences in children's matrix problem-solving abilities: evidence from eye movements
finding: 67 children aged 7-8. Better solvers looked longer at the matrix than the answers. Poor solvers looked longer at answers and kept re-examining the matrix after seeing options, read by the author as response elimination. Rows-and-columns count was the strongest predictor of accuracy.
numbers: N=67. Matrix latency, first-toggle latency, integration and rows/columns all correlated positively with accuracy; rows and columns strongest. Accuracy on the 22-item test fell from 97% to 30% across items (ceiling on the first 11 items).
limits: Small child sample, one test (CAS2). Cites Chen et al. (2016): toggling correlated positively with accuracy (r=.41) in children, which cuts against the rule that more toggling is bad.
agent_relevance: Toggling is not always bad. Checking a built answer against options (verify) differs from searching options (eliminate).

source: Weber, Koch, Spinath, Krieger & Greiff (2025) Log file times as indicators of structured figural matrix processing
finding: Computer-based figural matrices. Time spent between rules (planning a rule-by-rule solution) separated two clusters; only the speeding-up of inter-rule times over the test related to performance.
numbers: N=198. Three log-file times explained an extra 24.30% of test-score variance beyond total time on task.
limits: One construction-style test. Time-on-step measures, not eye movements.
agent_relevance: Per-rule step timing is a cheap signal that structured building took place; usable for our agent logs.

source: Becker et al. (2016) Preventing response elimination strategies improves the convergent validity of figural matrices
finding: Per Laurence & Macedo 2023: requiring people to build their own answer from given elements, so options cannot be eliminated, raised validity relative to the multiple-choice format. Original not opened.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Secondary report only. Title and year approximate.
agent_relevance: The strongest test-design analogue: remove the option list and force generation.

source: Arendasy & Sommer (2013) Reducing response elimination strategies enhances the construct validity of figural matrices
finding: Per Laurence & Macedo 2023: strategy changes what a matrix test measures. A redesigned answer-option format led to less response elimination. Original not opened.
numbers: Exact numbers not read.
limits: Secondary report only. Title approximate.
agent_relevance: Distractor design controls how much elimination is possible. The same holds for benchmark design.

source: Vakil & Lifshitz-Zehavi (2012) Solving the Raven Progressive Matrices by adults with intellectual disability with/without Down syndrome (with Curie et al. 2016)
finding: Per Laurence & Macedo 2023: people with intellectual disability or Down syndrome looked at answers sooner and made more matrix-answer toggles than typically developing peers. Curie et al. found the same on a 2x2 adaptation with two answers.
numbers: Group sizes and effect sizes not read.
limits: Secondary report only.
agent_relevance: An early look at options marks shallow analysis in every group. A scaffold can block it by hiding options.

source: Kucharsky et al. (2020) Hidden Markov model clustering of eye movements on Raven matrices
finding: Unsupervised clustering did not find a clean response-elimination class. It found row-wise vs column-wise scanning patterns. Known via Laurence & Macedo 2023.
numbers: Exact N not read.
limits: Failed to reproduce the two-strategy split with a data-driven method. Opened only via review. Author spelling approximate.
agent_relevance: Boundary on the whole topic: response elimination may be a frustrated attempt at construction, not a separate strategy.

source: Gonthier (2022) Cross-cultural differences in visuo-spatial processing and the culture-fairness of visuo-spatial intelligence tests
finding: Reviews how perception and handling of visual information varies across cultures and models seven steps of Raven solving. Concludes visuo-spatial tests are not culture-fair.
numbers: Review, no numbers used.
limits: Does not measure strategy directly.
agent_relevance: The strategy findings come from student samples; do not assume the build/eliminate split holds across populations.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) on digit matrices modelled on Raven's SPM. Both a generative answer (build, no options) and selection from options were tested. GPT-3 beat the mean of human students in both. Its profile across problem types resembled humans.
numbers: Humans N=40 UCLA students. Generative: odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.21-2.91, p=.005). Multiple-choice: OR 6.27 (CI 3.28-11.99, p=2.3e-8). Profile correlation r(30)=.39, p=.027. Best human got everything right.
limits: Text digit matrices, not images. Later counterfactual work shows brittleness (b25). Odds ratios only; raw accuracy was in a figure.
agent_relevance: The one LLM study to run both a no-options generative condition and a choice condition on matrices. The model's advantage over humans was larger with options, consistent with some gain from option access.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Counterfactual (permuted alphabet) variants of the letter-string analogies used by Webb et al. Humans stayed high; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 dropped sharply. Error types differ from humans.
numbers: Human errors: 38.59% alternate rules vs GPT-4 22% vs GPT-3 5.81%. GPT-3 and GPT-4 had over 30% of errors from wrong rules, humans about 15%. Human sample 46 per problem type.
limits: Letter strings, not matrices. Accuracy values read from plots.
agent_relevance: Success on familiar items may be retrieval, not construction. Test any scaffold on counterfactual and re-skinned items.

source: Gendron, Bao, Witbrock & Dobbie (2023) Large language models are not strong abstract reasoners
finding: Open-ended generation (no options) on abstract reasoning tasks including a text RAVEN. All tested LLMs scored low. MCQA models did slightly above random when choosing among options, and the authors note that choosing has an advantage over generating.
numbers: RAVEN-T open QA accuracy: GPT-4 0.410 (text) and 0.330 (symbolic); Text-Davinci-3 0.343 / 0.234; GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.226 / 0.161. Other sets, GPT-4: ARCT 0.119, BIG-Bench-F 0.514, PVR 0.177.
limits: Text and symbolic encodings, direct answers, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Generating an answer with no options (pure construction) is hard for LLMs. That is where a build scaffold should help most.

source: Hu, Ma, Liu, Wei & Bai (2021) Stratified Rule-Aware Network for Abstract Visual Reasoning (I-RAVEN)
finding: RAVEN's answer set leaks the answer: the correct option has the most common attribute values. Models that saw only the 8 options (no matrix) scored higher than models that saw the full problem. A rebuilt answer set (I-RAVEN) removed the leak. This is a machine response-elimination shortcut.
numbers: RAVEN: ResNet 53.4%, CoPINet 91.4%, context-blind ResNet 71.9%, context-blind CoPINet 94.2%. I-RAVEN: ResNet 40.3%, CoPINet 46.1%, context-blind ResNet 12.2%, context-blind CoPINet 14.2% (chance 12.5%).
limits: Trained networks, not LLMs. Shows the shortcut is in the benchmark data.
agent_relevance: Any matrix benchmark we use needs a choices-only baseline. An agent that gets credit through the answer-set trick is not building.

source: Balepur, Ravichander & Rudinger (2024) Artifacts or abduction: how do LLMs answer multiple-choice questions without the question?
finding: Four LLMs on ARC, MMLU and HellaSwag with the question removed. Choices-only beat a majority baseline in 11 of 12 cases, by up to 0.33 accuracy. Not explained by memorisation or single-option priors alone; models use how options relate. In 43 ARC cases the model inferred a question from choices; 42% matched the real one.
numbers: 11/12 cases above majority baseline; max gain 0.33. Few-shot 5 (MMLU) to 25 (ARC) examples. Question inference match 42% of 43.
limits: Text MCQ, not matrices. Inferring the question can be real reasoning, not only a shortcut.
agent_relevance: The LLM version of response elimination is real and strong. Hide options during the build phase to force the first strategy.

source: Myrzakhan, Bsharat & Shen (2024) Open-LLM-Leaderboard: from multi-choice to open-style questions
finding: Same questions in multiple-choice and open form. Every model drops sharply in open style, about 25 points on average.
numbers: GPT-4 average MCQ 88.69 vs open-style 61.31 over 9 datasets; MMLU 87.28 vs 74.77; HellaSwag 90.98 vs 24.35 (largest drop).
limits: Open-style answers were filtered and auto-judged, so part of the drop is a grading artefact. Not matrices.
agent_relevance: Estimates the lift the option list gives an LLM. Real reasoning ability is nearer the open-style figure.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Large language models are not robust multiple choice selectors; Pezeshkpour & Hruschka (2023) Large language models sensitivity to the order of options in multiple-choice questions
finding: Moving the correct option changes accuracy: models prefer particular option letters (Zheng, 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks). Pezeshkpour reports a 13% to 75% performance gap on reordering, and up to 8 points regained by calibration.
numbers: Zheng: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks, debiasing method PriDe. Pezeshkpour: gap about 13% to 75% across benchmarks; calibration gives up to 8 points.
limits: Position bias, not specific to matrices. Abstracts and introductions read only.
agent_relevance: Another surface-feature failure of option lists. Shuffle options and re-score as a check.

source: Cao et al. (2025) What is the visual cognition gap between humans and multimodal LLMs? (MaRs-VQA)
finding: Matrix-reasoning benchmark for multimodal LLMs. Best zero-shot model GPT-o1 52.29% vs human adults 81.00% on 4-option items. Adding option images to the question image raised GPT-4o from 24.58% to 33.96%. A multi-round step-by-step option-elimination prompt (with reflect and retry) raised GPT-4o from about 34% to 42%. Few-shot examples gave only 34% to 36%.
numbers: MaRs-VQA 4-option: GPT-4o 33.96, GPT-o1 52.29, Qwen2-VCog (fine-tuned) 72.71, human 81.00. RAVEN 8-option: human 84.41, fine-tuned model 31.96. Question image only: GPT-4o 24.58; with option images 33.96; with option descriptions 36.46. Fine-tuning lifted RAVEN only from 29.27 to 31.96 (shortcut features suspected).
limits: Prompt ablation is one model and one benchmark. The elimination prompt is slower and includes a reflect-and-retry loop, so the lift is not purely from elimination.
agent_relevance: The one measured LLM result on a matrix task where an elimination routine helps. For a weak visual model, elimination with reflection can be a real gain, unlike for humans.

source: Cai et al. (2025) MM-IQ: benchmarking human-like abstraction and reasoning in multimodal models
finding: 2,710 test items in 8 reasoning paradigms. Best multimodal models reached only 33.17% against 25% chance. A model trained by reinforcement learning on 4,776 items was competitive at a smaller size.
numbers: Best model 33.17% vs 25% chance, 4 options, 2,710 test items.
limits: Benchmark paper; human comparison figure not read in detail.
agent_relevance: Four-option IQ-style puzzles were near chance for the frontier models of that period, so elimination could not rescue them.

source: Srivastava, Jaarsveld & Sangani (2023) Verbal-analytical rather than visuo-spatial Raven's puzzle solving favors Raven's-like puzzle generation
finding: Links verbal-analytical solving (rule naming) rather than visuo-spatial solving to better creation of new Raven-like puzzles. Supports verbal rule-naming as part of effective construction.
numbers: Only abstract and introduction read; no figures extracted.
limits: Partly read. Sample size not recorded.
agent_relevance: Naming each rule in words is the construction step an LLM does best.

source: de Winter, Dodou & Eisma (2023) Responses to Raven matrices: governed by visual complexity and centrality
finding: Response time and fixation count on a 12-item APM were explained by low-level visual complexity and cell centrality, not only by strategy. A rival explanation for gaze-based strategy indices.
numbers: N=159, 12 items. Visual complexity correlated positively with mean response time and with fixations on the matrix.
limits: Short test. Indices like time-on-matrix may reflect perception load.
agent_relevance: Time spent on the stem is not proof of building. Check with an output such as a stated predicted answer.
